evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) – a bladed tool to plow the ground and to mark a border. As an alternative, a carpenter's square; according to the second interpretation, the character is related to the original meaning of 巨.
Unrelated to 巠 > 𢀖 and 壬.
An area word; compare Burmese ခိုင်း (hkuing:, “to order or ask someone to do something”), Old Mon kloñ (kloɲ, “to work”), Old Mon klon (klon, “to have charge of cultivation”) (Schuessler, 2007).
Etymologically the same word as 功 (OC *koːŋ, “merit; achievement”) and 攻 (OC *koːŋ, *kuːŋ, “to attack”). The senses evolved in the following manner: 工 (“work, artisan”) > 功 (“merit; achievement”); 工 (“to work”) > 攻 (“to attack”) (ibid.).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義源流通解 / graphic analysis
evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone and bronze forms as resembling a tool. It reports one proposal that the graph depicts a bladed tool, perhaps with a carpenter’s-square function at its upper part; it also records proposals that 工 depicts a square or a building tool. These are competing identifications, not a settled identification of the object.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：工

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 甲骨文、金文、戰國文字用例及形義通解
evidence.text: The database says the lower horizontal stroke in early bronze forms is thicker, and compares it to the blade-like stroke of 王 in forms interpreted as an axe. It reports that oracle-bone occurrences include a state or place name; another proposed use denotes status, a low-ranking official, or craftspeople, with cited examples 多工 in Heji 19433 and 百工 in Tunnan 2525. Bronze inscriptions use 工 in an official title interpreted as 司空 and in 工師, and also cite inscriptions where 工 is used for 功, ‘achievement’. The entry does not date each cited artifact in the displayed text, so these examples cannot by themselves establish the first occurrence of each sense.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：工

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義源流通解 / interpretation of borrowing
evidence.text: The database identifies 工 as a phonetic loan for 貢 in oracle-bone examples 工(貢)冊 in Heji 38310 and 工(貢)父甲三牛 in Heji 27462, glossed as presenting records and offering three cattle. This is a reported whole-graph loan in those contexts; it does not make 工 a sound component in its own graph.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：工

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry reports bronze-inscription uses of 工 for 功, ‘achievement’, citing 班簋, 中山王方壺, and 沈子它簋, and a Warring States bamboo-slip example in 上博竹書一《孔子詩論》簡5, where 工 is read as 功 in a context about accomplishment. These support early graphic borrowing or interchange between 工 and 功 in the cited contexts. They do not, by themselves, prove a complete semantic sequence from tool to work to achievement.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：工

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, text of 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.field: 說文解字 工 entry; commentary
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry says 工 means 巧飾 and explains the form as a person having 規矩, comparing it with 巫. The entry also records a graph identified as ancient 工 formed with 彡. Duan Yucai reads 巧飾 in relation to skilled finishing and gives an extended gloss that anything done well is 工. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s original referent.
evidence.title: 說文解字「工」

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 工 entry (historical-form and pronunciation tables)
evidence.field: Middle Chinese and Old Chinese pronunciation
evidence.text: For 工, the entry gives Guangyun fanqie 古紅切, Middle Chinese Baxter transcription kuwng, and lists reconstructions including Zhengzhang /kuŋ/; it gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤoŋ and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *koːŋ. These are reconstructions in named systems, not direct ancient recordings. The same page lists modern Standard Mandarin gōng and Standard Cantonese gung1.
evidence.title: 工 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 工 entry (Baxter–Sagart table)
evidence.text: The table gives two readings for 工, glossed officer and work, with the same modern Beijing reading gōng, Middle Chinese ‹kuwng›, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese /*kˤoŋ/. This page supplies no distinct early sound for a depicted tool, and therefore cannot establish the name or pronunciation of the object proposed as the graph’s referent.
evidence.title: 工 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 工 entry (Zhengzhang phonetic-series table)
evidence.text: The entry places 工, 功, and 攻 in Zhengzhang’s 工 phonetic series and gives 工 and 功 as *koːŋ, with 攻 *koːŋ or *kuːŋ. This supports close reconstructed sound correspondence within that system. It does not alone establish that the meanings ‘work’, ‘achievement’, and ‘attack’ descend from one word, or determine the semantic path.
evidence.title: 工 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 工 entry (Chinese pronunciation and definition sections)
evidence.text: The entry lists Standard Mandarin gōng (Pinyin), Standard Cantonese gung1 (Jyutping), and the contemporary senses labour/work. The dossier separately supplies Korean kong, Vietnamese công, and Japanese on-readings, but no externally inspected source in this research established their historical transmission or earliest attestations.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The graph's exact depicted object remains disputed: the inspected paleographic database reports a bladed tool with possible square function, a square interpretation, and a building-tool proposal. No inspected primary artifact image or specialist publication resolved the identification.

No independently recoverable name or pronunciation for the proposed depicted tool was found. The character's own reconstructed pronunciation (*kˤoŋ in Baxter–Sagart; *koːŋ in Zhengzhang) cannot establish the object's name; the tool-pictograph account does not require a sound loan, so an object-name match is not established or needed here.

The opened paleographic entry lists oracle-bone and bronze artifact identifiers but does not date them; an earliest dated attestation for each sense (tool, place/state name, official/status, craft worker, work, achievement, and 貢 loan) remains unverified.

The semantic path from a tool graph to skilled work, worker, work/labor, skill, and achievement is not established as one chronological chain by the inspected sources. Shuowen's 巧飾 account and the modern paleographic tool analysis conflict in their accounts of the graph's original meaning.

The early official/status use and later craft/work uses should not be collapsed. The sources inspected do not establish whether they are semantically related, homonymous, or reflect graphic loan in all contexts.

The reported 工(貢) examples are whole-graph loans for 貢, distinct from 工 serving as a phonetic component in derived characters. Their exact dates and the phonological basis at the time of borrowing were not established.

工, 功, and 攻 have close readings in the cited reconstruction tables, but no independently inspected primary source established the dossier's proposed semantic etymologies connecting their word senses. A shared or similar reconstructed sound alone does not prove that etymology.

No sound component occurs inside 工 itself, so there is no component pronunciation/origin relation to classify for this character. The distinct shape 彡 in the Shuowen-reported ancient form 𢒄 is explicitly described there as part of that alternate graph, but the inspected sources do not establish it as an ancestor of 工.
The imported dossier's Burmese and Old Mon comparisons and the claim that 工 is an Austroasiatic area word were not independently verified in this research.

Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese readings are present in the dossier, but their dated transmission histories and earliest attestations were not investigated; Chinese spelling readings alone cannot establish a Japanese-origin account.

The precise object depicted by the early 工 graph remains disputed: the inspected paleographic source records a bladed tool with a possible square function, a square interpretation, and a building-tool interpretation.

The proposed graph-as-tool account does not establish the spoken name or pronunciation of the depicted object. 工’s reconstructed pronunciation cannot independently identify that object’s name; no separate name evidence was found.

The CUHK entry lists artifact identifiers but does not date each one in its displayed text. The earliest dated attestation for the tool graph, place or state name, official/status sense, craft occupation, work, achievement, and 貢 loan remains unverified.
The semantic route from proposed tool image to craft, worker, work, skill, and achievement is not established as one chronology. Shuowen’s 巧飾 explanation differs from the modern tool analysis.

The reported 工(貢) forms are whole-graph loans, separate from any sound-component analysis; no early borrowing pronunciation comparison or independently established 貢 sound evidence was found in the inspected pages.

工 has no internal sound component to classify. Shuowen’s 𢒄 is recorded as an alternate ancient graph with 彡, but the inspected sources do not establish whether it is an ancestor, variant, or other relation to 工.

The official Xiaoxuetang 工 query did not yield inspectable individual candidate labels or image URLs in the browser tool. The CUHK-linked image endpoints likewise lacked inspectable provenance. Thus no image candidate met the identity and reuse-provenance threshold.

limitations.text: No historical glyph image can be selected: the available research does not identify an inspectable image of 工 with verified form identity and provenance. The early graph’s proposed object is also disputed, with interpretations including a bladed tool, a square, and a building tool.
